title: Language core: exceptions, resources and functional style
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Checked vs unchecked, try-with-resources and suppressed exceptions, try/except/else/finally and context managers, plus streams, Optional, groupingBy, generators, comprehensions and lazy evaluation.
source: Oracle Java Tutorials: exceptions, java.util.stream docs; JLS 14.20; Python docs: errors, contextlib, itertools; Real Python; Baeldung

questions.prompt: Write a Java method static String firstLine(Path p) throws IOException that returns the first line of a text file and always closes the reader, using try-with-resources.
questions.starter: static String firstLine(Path p) throws IOException {

checks.label: opens a reader/scanner on the path
reads a line and returns it

questions.explanation: Resources declared in the parentheses must implement AutoCloseable and are closed automatically, even on exceptions. Files.lines(p) in a try-with-resources is equally valid.

The return value is evaluated and saved before finally runs, so reassigning the local x in finally cannot change it. (A return inside finally would override it and also swallow exceptions, which is why it is a code smell.) Verified by running it.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In try-with-resources, resources are closed in the reverse order of their declaration.
questions.reason: A resource used in try-with-resources must implement AutoCloseable.

whys.a: R is true but it does not explain the ordering; the reverse order exists because later resources may depend on earlier ones.
whys.b: Correct: both statements are true, but the AutoCloseable requirement is unrelated to the closing order.
whys.c: R is true: the compiler rejects other types.
whys.d: A is true: JLS 14.20.3 specifies reverse order.

questions.explanation: Reverse closing mirrors construction, e.g. close the BufferedReader before the FileReader it wraps. Exceptions from close() are added as suppressed exceptions to the primary one.

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about Java exceptions.

options.text: If the try body throws A and close() then throws B, A propagates and B is attached via getSuppressed().
options.why: Correct: this is how try-with-resources avoids losing the original failure.

options.text: A custom class that extends RuntimeException is an unchecked exception.
options.why: Correct: the compiler does not force callers to catch or declare it.
OutOfMemoryError is an Error, which is a sibling of Exception under Throwable.

options.text: catch (IOException | Exception e) compiles as a multi-catch.
options.why: It does not: alternatives in a multi-catch must not be subclasses of one another. (Statement is false, so do not select it.)

options.text: A finally block still runs if the try block calls System.exit(0).
options.why: The JVM halts, so finally is skipped.

questions.explanation: Unchecked exceptions signal programming errors; checked exceptions model recoverable conditions the caller must handle. Do not swallow exceptions silently, and wrap with a cause to keep the stack trace.

questions.prompt: Write a Python context manager function opened(path) that opens a text file, yields it, and always closes it, so it can be used as: with opened("a.txt") as f: ...  (write the function only).
questions.explanation: A class defining __enter__ and __exit__ is equivalent. Putting yield inside with open(path) as f: also closes the file. Without try/finally an exception in the with-body would skip the cleanup after yield.

questions.prompt:
What does this Python code print?
def f():
    try:
        return "try"
    finally:
        print("finally", end=" ")
print(f())
What is the output?

options.why: finally runs before the function actually hands control back, so it prints first.
Correct: finally prints during the return, then print outputs the returned value.
The finally clause always runs on the way out, so something else is printed too.
The returned string "try" is still printed by the outer print call.

questions.explanation: try/except/else/finally: else runs only if no exception was raised, finally always runs. (Verified by running it.)

questions.text: In Python, the {1} clause of a try statement runs only when no exception occurred, and the {2} clause always runs; to re-raise with the original as the cause, write raise NewError from {3}.
questions.explanation: else keeps the guarded region small so that only the risky call is covered by except. raise X from e sets __cause__; raise X from None suppresses the chain display.

questions.prompt: Match each tool to what it does.

right.text: Declares the checked exceptions a method may let propagate
Closes AutoCloseable resources and records close failures as suppressed
Calls __enter__ on entry and __exit__ even when the body fails
Turns a checked exception into an unchecked one automatically

questions.explanation: Python has no checked exceptions; Java forces handling of checked ones, which is why many libraries (Spring) prefer unchecked exceptions.

questions.prompt: What does Stream.of(1,2,3,4,5,6).filter(n -> n % 2 == 0).map(n -> n * n).reduce(0, Integer::sum) evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Even numbers 2, 4, 6 are squared to 4, 16, 36 and summed: 56.

questions.prompt: Given List<String> words, write a Java stream expression that builds Map<Integer, List<String>> byLength grouping the words by their length.
questions.explanation: Add a downstream collector for aggregation, e.g. groupingBy(String::length, Collectors.counting()). A plain loop with computeIfAbsent also works but is not what the stem asks.

questions.prompt:
What is printed?
Stream.of("a", "b", "c")
  .peek(s -> System.out.print("p" + s + " "))
  .filter(s -> !s.equals("b"))
  .findFirst();
What is the output?

options.why: Intermediate operations are lazy and findFirst short-circuits; the pipeline does not touch every element.
Correct: "a" passes the filter and findFirst stops the pipeline at once, so b and c are never visited.
The first matching element ends the pipeline before b is pulled.
findFirst is a terminal operation, so the pipeline runs.

questions.explanation: Streams are pull-based and lazy: nothing happens until a terminal operation, and short-circuiting ops (findFirst, limit, anyMatch) stop early. A stream also cannot be reused: a second terminal operation throws IllegalStateException. (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt:
What does this Python print?
g = (x * x for x in range(3))
print(list(g), list(g), sum(g))
What is the output?

options.why: That would be true for a list, not a generator; the iterator is consumed by the first list(g).
sum(g) also sees an exhausted generator.
Correct: the first list drains the generator, so the second list and the sum see nothing.
Python does not raise here; an exhausted generator simply yields nothing more.

questions.explanation: Generators are one-shot iterators. If you need two passes, build a list, tee with itertools.tee, or recreate the generator. (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt: Write a Python generator function chunks(seq, n) that yields successive slices of length n from the sequence (the last one may be shorter).

checks.label: steps through with range or a loop

questions.explanation: itertools.batched(it, n) does this in Python 3.12+. A generator keeps memory flat because it produces one chunk at a time.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In Java, optional.orElse(expensive()) calls expensive() even when the Optional already holds a value.
questions.reason: Java evaluates method arguments eagerly before the method is invoked.

whys.a: Correct: arguments are evaluated first, so use orElseGet(() -> expensive()) to defer the work.
whys.b: R is the reason for A, not an unrelated fact.

questions.explanation: orElseGet takes a Supplier and runs it only when empty. Also avoid Optional.get() without a check; prefer orElseThrow, map and ifPresent.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Calling a Python generator function runs none of its body until the first next() call.
questions.reason: A generator function computes all of its values into a list when it is called.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (the call just creates a generator object); R is false, since values are produced lazily one at a time.

questions.explanation: That laziness lets generators model infinite sequences and stream large files without loading them into memory.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In Python 3, the loop variable of a list comprehension remains visible in the enclosing scope after the comprehension ends.
questions.reason: In Python 2, list comprehension variables leaked into the enclosing scope.

whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: Python 3 gives comprehensions their own scope (A is false); R is true for Python 2.

questions.explanation: A for loop statement still leaks its variable; only comprehensions and generator expressions have their own scope.
